title: The Gold Cup Shattered, the Scroll Sunk in the Euphrates
summary: The oracle against Babylon continues and reaches its end. The LORD stirs up the Medes against the city that made the nations drunk, calls his people to flee, contrasts himself as Maker of all things with Babylon's lifeless idols, and promises that the destroying mountain will become a charred ruin. The chapter closes with a dated sign-act: Jeremiah sends a scroll of these words to Babylon with Seraiah, to be read aloud and sunk in the Euphrates as a sign that Babylon will sink and never rise.
story: This chapter completes the long oracle against Babylon begun in chapter 50 and brings the words of Jeremiah to a close (verse 64). The prophet who told Judah to submit to Babylon and told the exiles to seek the welfare of the city where they lived now says that Babylon's time is limited and that God's people must not make themselves at home there forever. The two messages fit together. Submission was for a season; the season would end when God judged the empire for what it had done in Zion. The final scene, dated to Zedekiah's fourth year, shows that Jeremiah announced Babylon's fall years before Jerusalem's own collapse, at the same time as he was urging Zedekiah not to rebel. Chapter 52, a historical appendix, follows.
historical:
The Medes, named in verses 11 and 28, were an Iranian people whose kingdom had joined Babylon in destroying the Assyrian capital Nineveh in 612 BC. By the middle of the sixth century the Median kingdom had been taken over by Cyrus of Persia, whose combined Medo-Persian army took Babylon in 539 BC. Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz (verse 27) were peoples of the mountains north of Mesopotamia (Ararat is Urartu, around Lake Van in eastern Turkey), all of which came under Median control. Babylon's own features appear throughout: its many waters (the Euphrates and a network of canals), its thick walls, and its high gates, all famous in the ancient world.

Verses 59 to 64 are dated to the fourth year of Zedekiah, about 594/593 BC. That year envoys from Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon had met in Jerusalem to plan revolt (27:3), and Zedekiah may have gone to Babylon to reassure Nebuchadnezzar of his loyalty. Seraiah son of Neriah was a royal officer (the quartermaster, responsible for the king's lodging on the road) and the brother of Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe, whose father and grandfather are named the same way in 32:12. The visit to Babylon is mentioned only here.
cultural:
Babylon is pictured as “a gold cup in the hand of the LORD, making the whole earth drunk” (verse 7). A cup of wine was a sign of hospitality and celebration; in the prophets it became the cup of God's wrath, which reduces the nations to staggering helplessness. Babylon was the cup's rim, glittering and valuable, but still only a vessel in God's hand. Verses 20 to 23 call Babylon God's war club, and the ninefold refrain with you I shatter reads like a war chant.

Two names in the chapter are coded. Leb-kamai (verse 1) and Sheshach (verse 41) are formed by atbash, a Hebrew letter-substitution in which the first letter of the alphabet is swapped for the last, the second for the second-to-last, and so on. By that method Leb-kamai stands for Kasdim (Chaldeans) and Sheshach for Babel. The code was probably a form of wordplay rather than secrecy, since both chapters also name Babylon openly. The closing sign-act also drew on familiar practice: prophets sometimes acted out their message (Jeremiah had broken a clay jar in chapter 19 and worn a yoke in chapter 27), and a written word sealed and sunk carried the weight of a performed curse.
literary: The chapter is poetry, like chapter 50, and shares its structure of alternating scenes: Babylon's fall, calls to flee, and words of comfort to Zion. It includes a hymn to the Creator (verses 15 to 19) that repeats Jeremiah 10:12-16 almost word for word, placing the LORD's power and wisdom over against idols that have no breath. At the center Zion speaks in her own voice: Nebuchadnezzar devoured me, swallowed me like a monster, and vomited me out (verses 34 and 35). The LORD answers by promising to plead her case and to make Bel spew out what he swallowed (verse 44), a direct reversal of her complaint. The chapter closes with prose (verses 59 to 64), a narrative of the sign-act, and the editorial note that marks the end of the words of Jeremiah.

outline.t: The destroyer stirred up; flee from the doomed city
The Medes aroused: the vengeance for the temple
The Maker of all things and the worthless idols
The war club broken; the destroying mountain burned
The nations summoned; the city captured end to end
Zion's complaint and the LORD's answer: Bel made to disgorge
Come out of her, My people; the walls leveled
The scroll read in Babylon and sunk in the Euphrates

doctrines.note: The hymn of verses 15 to 19 grounds the whole oracle in creation: “The LORD made the earth by His power; He established the world by His wisdom.” The one who made the world can bring down any power in it, and idols made by goldsmiths are a fraud.

Babylon was a gold cup and a war club in the LORD's hand. God used a proud empire to carry out his judgment without approving its pride, and then held it to account. History moves under his hand even when the actors do not know him.

“Come out of her, My people” (verse 45) calls God's people to refuse to be absorbed by the empire that has held them. Revelation 18:4 takes up this call for the church, which lives in the world but must not share its idolatry.

words.note: Mappets, war club or shatterer, a heavy weapon for smashing. Used only here in this form, it names Babylon's role: God's instrument for breaking nations. The repeated verb in verses 20 to 23 comes from the same root, which is why the refrain sounds like blows falling.

Cheleq, portion or share, especially an inheritance of land. Calling the LORD “The Portion of Jacob” (verse 19) means that Israel's true inheritance is God himself. Levites received no land because the LORD was their portion (Numbers 18:20), and the psalms and Lamentations 3:24 use the same language of personal trust.

Sepher, a written document or scroll. Jeremiah's words were written down more than once (chapter 36), and here the written word itself becomes part of the prophecy: read aloud, then weighted with a stone and sunk. Writing gave the prophecy permanence even when the prophet was absent.

Neqamah, vengeance, meaning justice restored by the rightful authority. Verse 11 calls Babylon's fall the vengeance of the LORD, the vengeance for His temple. God does not ignore the desecration of his house or the blood of his people.

christ: Revelation draws heavily on this chapter. The woman called Babylon holds a golden cup (Revelation 17:4); a voice from heaven cries come out of her, my people (Revelation 18:4, echoing verse 45); heaven and earth rejoice over her fall (Revelation 18:20, echoing verse 48); and an angel throws a great millstone into the sea, saying Babylon will be thrown down and found no more (Revelation 18:21), a clear echo of Seraiah's stone and scroll. For John, Babylon has become the name for every power that seduces and persecutes God's people, and its end is certain because of the victory of the Lamb. The chapter's picture of the LORD as the Portion of Jacob also finds its fullness in Christ, in whom believers receive an inheritance that cannot perish.

hard.q: How should we read the calls for Babylon's total destruction, including young men and whole armies?
hard.a: The language is harsh, and readers should feel its weight. Several things are worth saying. First, these are words of the victims. Zion's complaint in verses 34 and 35 is the voice of a people whose temple was burned and whose children starved, and the prophets let that grief and anger speak to God rather than turn into private revenge. Second, the vengeance belongs to God; the people are told to flee, not to fight (verses 6, 45, and 50). Third, the images are the conventional language of ancient war oracles and curse texts, which described defeat in total terms; Babylon was not, in fact, massacred in 539 BC. Some interpreters stress that the poem is about the end of an empire's power rather than a blueprint for slaughter. Others add that the New Testament, which takes up this language in Revelation, reserves judgment to God and calls believers to love their enemies. The chapter does insist that evil on the scale of empire will be answered, and a reader who has been on the receiving end of such evil may find that comfort rather than a scandal.

questions: Babylon's idols had no breath in them (verse 17). What things in your life promise security or meaning but have no life to give?
“Come out of her, My people” was a call to leave a comfortable exile. Where might God be calling you not to settle too comfortably into the values of the culture around you?
Jeremiah wrote this scroll during years when Babylon looked unbeatable. How does knowing that God has set limits to present powers change how you live under them?
